claim: The descending pain modulatory system (DPMS) constitutes a network of widely distributed brain regions whose integrated function is essential for effective modulation of sensory input to the central nervous system and behavioural responses to pain.
source: The descending pain modulatory system (DPMS) constitutes a network of widely distributed brain regions whose integrated function is essential for effective modulation of sensory input to the central nervous system and behavioural responses to pain.
evidence: This is a general statement about the DPMS that draws from established scientific understanding of pain modulation systems.

claim: Animal studies demonstrate that young rodents have an immature DPMS.
source: Animal studies demonstrate that young rodents have an immature DPMS, but comparable studies have not been conducted in human infants.
evidence: This claim references animal studies as the source of evidence.

claim: Comparable studies to those in young rodents have not been conducted in human infants.
source: Animal studies demonstrate that young rodents have an immature DPMS, but comparable studies have not been conducted in human infants.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of prior research in human infants.

claim: Pain-related brain activity in newborn infants is similar to that observed in adults.
source: In Goksan et al. (2015) we used functional MRI (fMRI) to show that pain-related brain activity in newborn infants is similar to that observed in adults.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Greater pre-stimulus functional network connectivity across the DPMS was significantly associated with lower noxious-evoked brain activity (p = 0.0004, r = -0.86, n = 13).
source: Greater pre-stimulus functional network connectivity across the DPMS was significantly associated with lower noxious-evoked brain activity (p = 0.0004, r = -0.86, n = 13), suggesting that in newborn infants the DPMS may regulate the magnitude of noxious-evoked brain activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data collected in the study.

claim: In newborn infants the DPMS may regulate the magnitude of noxious-evoked brain activity.
source: Greater pre-stimulus functional network connectivity across the DPMS was significantly associated with lower noxious-evoked brain activity (p = 0.0004, r = -0.86, n = 13), suggesting that in newborn infants the DPMS may regulate the magnitude of noxious-evoked brain activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data showing the relationship between DPMS connectivity and brain activity.

claim: In adults, pain perception is modulated by the descending pain modulatory system (DPMS).
source: In adults, pain perception is modulated by the descending pain modulatory system (DPMS), allowing environmental, contextual and cognitive factors to influence our pain experiences (McMahon et al., 2013; Ossipov et al., 2010; Tracey and Mantyh, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The DPMS allows environmental, contextual and cognitive factors to influence pain experiences.
source: In adults, pain perception is modulated by the descending pain modulatory system (DPMS), allowing environmental, contextual and cognitive factors to influence our pain experiences (McMahon et al., 2013; Ossipov et al., 2010; Tracey and Mantyh, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The DPMS comprises a network of cortical and subcortical brain regions that can facilitate or inhibit nociceptive afferent brain input via brainstem nuclei.
source: The DPMS comprises a network of cortical and subcortical brain regions that can facilitate or inhibit nociceptive afferent brain input via brainstem nuclei (Ossipov et al., 2010; Tracey, 2010; Zhuo and Gebhart, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The functional connectivity of the DPMS is altered in adult chronic pain conditions such as migraine, back pain, fibromyalgia and painful diabetic neuropathy.
source: The functional connectivity of the DPMS is altered in adult chronic pain conditions such as migraine, back pain, fibromyalgia and painful diabetic neuropathy (Jensen et al., 2012; Mainero et al., 2011; Segerdahl et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2014), and transient alterations in DPMS connectivity influences pain perception.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Transient alterations in DPMS connectivity influences pain perception.
source: The functional connectivity of the DPMS is altered in adult chronic pain conditions such as migraine, back pain, fibromyalgia and painful diabetic neuropathy (Jensen et al., 2012; Mainero et al., 2011; Segerdahl et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2014), and transient alterations in DPMS connectivity influences pain perception.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Pre-stimulus functional connectivity between the anterior insula (AI) and the periaqueductal gray (PAG) relates to whether or not a noxious stimulus is perceived as painful.
source: For example, pre-stimulus functional connectivity between the anterior insula (AI) and the periaqueductal gray (PAG) relates to whether or not a noxious stimulus is perceived as painful (Ploner et al., 2010), and pre-stimulus activity in the insular and anterior cingulate cortices (ACC) is predictive of subsequent pain intensity ratings (Boly et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Pre-stimulus activity in the insular and anterior cingulate cortices (ACC) is predictive of subsequent pain intensity ratings.
source: For example, pre-stimulus functional connectivity between the anterior insula (AI) and the periaqueductal gray (PAG) relates to whether or not a noxious stimulus is perceived as painful (Ploner et al., 2010), and pre-stimulus activity in the insular and anterior cingulate cortices (ACC) is predictive of subsequent pain intensity ratings (Boly et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Anticipatory brainstem activity in adults has been shown to predict changes in insula activity evoked by noxious thermal stimulation.
source: Furthermore, anticipatory brainstem activity in adults has been shown to predict changes in insula activity evoked by noxious thermal stimulation (Fairhurst et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific study.

claim: Evidence from animal studies suggests that infant descending pain modulation is immature.
source: Evidence from animal studies suggests that infant descending pain modulation is immature (Hathway et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to animal studies.

claim: During the first 3 postnatal weeks, anatomical descending projections to the dorsal horn are physically present in rat pups.
source: During the first 3 postnatal weeks, anatomical descending projections to the dorsal horn are physically present; however, physiological inhibition of nociceptive input is ineffective or absent in rat pups (Hathway et al., 2009; Fitzgerald and Koltzenburg, 1986; Hathway et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to animal studies.

claim: Physiological inhibition of nociceptive input is ineffective or absent in rat pups during the first 3 postnatal weeks.
source: During the first 3 postnatal weeks, anatomical descending projections to the dorsal horn are physically present; however, physiological inhibition of nociceptive input is ineffective or absent in rat pups (Hathway et al., 2009; Fitzgerald and Koltzenburg, 1986; Hathway et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to animal studies.

claim: The brainstem nuclei in the rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM) are the principle source of descending projections to the dorsal horn.
source: Moreover, the brainstem nuclei in the rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM), which are the principle source of these projections, exclusively facilitate nociceptive spinal activity, rather than exerting more adult-like biphasic inhibitory and facilitatory nociceptive control (Hathway et al., 2009; Schwaller et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In neonatal rodents, the brainstem nuclei in the RVM exclusively facilitate nociceptive spinal activity, rather than exerting more adult-like biphasic inhibitory and facilitatory nociceptive control.
source: Moreover, the brainstem nuclei in the rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM), which are the principle source of these projections, exclusively facilitate nociceptive spinal activity, rather than exerting more adult-like biphasic inhibitory and facilitatory nociceptive control (Hathway et al., 2009; Schwaller et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to animal studies.

claim: In the human infant, spinal reflexes are uncoordinated, exaggerated and prolonged.
source: In the human infant, spinal reflexes are uncoordinated, exaggerated and prolonged (Andrews and Fitzgerald, 1994; Cornelissen et al., 2013; Hartley et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Nociceptive reflexes are refined postnatally in infants born prematurely.
source: Nociceptive reflexes are refined postnatally in infants born prematurely, and by term age, infant reflexes have lower amplitude and shorter duration compared with premature infants (Cornelissen et al., 2013; Hartley et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: By term age, infant reflexes have lower amplitude and shorter duration compared with premature infants.
source: Nociceptive reflexes are refined postnatally in infants born prematurely, and by term age, infant reflexes have lower amplitude and shorter duration compared with premature infants (Cornelissen et al., 2013; Hartley et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: During the postnatal developmental period, the refinement of spinal cord excitability is concomitant with the maturation of nociceptive brain activity.
source: During this developmental period, the postnatal refinement of spinal cord excitability is concomitant with the maturation of nociceptive brain activity (Hartley et al., 2016), leading to the possibility that in the newborn term infant, the brain regions involved in descending pain modulation may be influential in modifying pain behaviour and experience.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: In the newborn term infant, the brain regions involved in descending pain modulation may be influential in modifying pain behaviour and experience.
source: During this developmental period, the postnatal refinement of spinal cord excitability is concomitant with the maturation of nociceptive brain activity (Hartley et al., 2016), leading to the possibility that in the newborn term infant, the brain regions involved in descending pain modulation may be influential in modifying pain behaviour and experience.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the cited developmental observations.

claim: Patterns of noxious-evoked brain activity in the infant are similar to those observed in the adult, and include both sensory and affective brain regions.
source: In our previous paper, we used fMRI to demonstrate that patterns of noxious-evoked brain activity in the infant are similar to those observed in the adult, and include both sensory and affective brain regions (Goksan et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Changes in noxious-evoked BOLD activity can be used as objective surrogate measures to make inferences about pain experiences in non-verbal infants.
source: Given we cannot measure subjective pain experience in non-verbal infants, we are reliant on objective surrogate measures such as changes in noxious-evoked BOLD activity to make inferences about pain experiences (Baumgärtner et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2008; Maihöfner and Handwerker, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and represents a methodological approach.

claim: Mild experimental noxious stimulation was applied to the infant's foot using a 128 mN PinPrick stimulator.
source: Mild experimental noxious stimulation was applied to the infant's foot using a 128 mN PinPrick stimulator.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method used in the study.

claim: The DPMS Network comprised the bilateral AI, ACC, amygdala (AMY), RVM, PAG, and the middle frontal gyri (mFG) situated within the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex.
source: The DPMS Network comprised the bilateral AI, ACC, amygdala (AMY), RVM, PAG, and the middle frontal gyri (mFG) situated within the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the brain regions selected for analysis based on established knowledge of the DPMS.

claim: The DPMS Network includes the main brain structures identified in the adult DPMS.
source: This includes the main brain structures identified in the adult DPMS (McMahon et al., 2013; Schweinhardt and Bushnell, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The Control Network comprised the bilateral calcarine cortices (CAL), caudate (CAU), hippocampus (HIP), pontine nuclei (PON), recti gyri (RGY) and the supplementary motor areas (SMA).
source: The brain regions in the Control Network are the bilateral calcarine cortices (CAL), caudate (CAU), hippocampus (HIP), pontine nuclei (PON), recti gyri (RGY) and the supplementary motor areas (SMA) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the brain regions selected for the control network analysis.

claim: The Default Mode Network has been identified in adults and term infants.
source: As an additional control, the Default Mode Network (an established network that has been identified in adults and term infants) (Doria et al., 2010; Raichle, 2015) allowed us to test the specificity of the relationship between the pre-stimulus functional connectivity of the DPMS and the noxious-evoked BOLD activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The Default Mode Network included the posterior cingulate cortex (PCC), the inferior parietal lobules (IPL) and the medial superior frontal gyrus (mSFG) situated within the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC).
source: The Default Mode Network included the posterior cingulate cortex (PCC), the inferior parietal lobules (IPL) and the medial superior frontal gyrus (mSFG) situated within the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This describes the brain regions selected for the Default Mode Network analysis.

claim: The overall mean pre-stimulus functional connectivity was not significantly different between the DPMS Network and the Control Network.
source: This was not significantly different between the DPMS Network and the Control Network (mean pre-stimulus functional connectivity: DPMS Network = 0.08 ± 0.10; Control Network = 0.15 ± 0.12).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The functional connectivity of the Default Mode Network was significantly greater than connectivity within the DPMS and the Control Network (p = 0.0014).
source: Unsurprisingly, given that the Default Mode Network is a canonical network that has been identified in both adult and infant resting state data (Doria et al., 2010; Raichle, 2015), the functional connectivity of the Default Mode Network was significantly greater (mean pre-stimulus functional connectivity: Default Mode Network = 0.24 ± 0.18) than connectivity within the DPMS and the Control Network (p = 0.0014, repeated measures ANOVA, Tukey post-hoc comparison of DPMS and Control Network: p = 0.06, Default Mode Network and DPMS: p < 0.001, Default Mode Network and Control Network: p = 0.047).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the data.

claim: Positive clusters of noxious-evoked BOLD activity were identified in the bilateral postcentral gyrus (somatosensory cortices), thalamus, anterior cingulate cortex and contralateral posterior insular cortex.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Goksan et al., 2015; Williams et al., 2015), we identified positive clusters of noxious-evoked BOLD activity in the bilateral postcentral gyrus (somatosensory cortices), thalamus, anterior cingulate cortex and contralateral posterior insular cortex (Figure 2, Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data and is consistent with prior research.

claim: Clusters of activity can be identified in the medial surface of the somatosensory cortex, which encodes the somatotopic foot representation.
source: For example, clusters of activity can now be identified in the medial surface of the somatosensory cortex, which encodes the somatotopic foot representation (Figure 2 and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data and anatomical knowledge.

claim: The statistical cluster-defining threshold has increased from z = 2.3 to z = 3.1, to account for potential inflation in family wise error rates that have been observed across a broad range of MRI studies.
source: Importantly, the statistical cluster-defining threshold has increased from z = 2.3 to z = 3.1, to account for potential inflation in family wise error rates that have been observed across a broad range of MRI studies (Eklund et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes a methodological improvement based on cited research.

claim: The brain regions identified in this more stringent analysis represent the most robustly activated clusters of noxious-evoked brain activity in the infant.
source: The brain regions identified in this more stringent analysis represent the most robustly activated clusters of noxious-evoked brain activity in the infant, and are consistent with those most commonly reported in adults (Tracey and Mantyh, 2007).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data analysis results.

claim: The brain regions identified are consistent with those most commonly reported in adults.
source: The brain regions identified in this more stringent analysis represent the most robustly activated clusters of noxious-evoked brain activity in the infant, and are consistent with those most commonly reported in adults (Tracey and Mantyh, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The infant pattern of pain-related brain activity is similar to that observed in adults.
source: Our previous report that the infant pattern of pain-related brain activity is similar to that observed in adults is reconfirmed here (Goksan et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by the current data and citation to prior work.

claim: There was a significant inverse relationship between the magnitude of pre-stimulus DPMS functional connectivity and the percentage change in noxious-evoked BOLD activity (r = -0.86, p = 0.0004, β = -0.74).
source: There was a significant inverse relationship between the magnitude of pre-stimulus DPMS functional connectivity and the percentage change in noxious-evoked BOLD activity (Pearson correlation coefficient (r) = -0.86, p = 0.0004, parameter estimate (β) = -0.74, linear model also included gestational age in weeks as an explanatory variable, Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Infants with greater functional connectivity across their DPMS Network prior to noxious stimulation had lower noxious-evoked brain activity.
source: Infants with greater functional connectivity across their DPMS Network prior to noxious stimulation had lower noxious-evoked brain activity.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical relationship found in the data.

claim: The mean functional connectivity in the Control Network was not related to the mean change in noxious-evoked BOLD activity (r = -0.36, p = 0.26, β = -0.25).
source: In contrast, the mean functional connectivity in the Control Network and in the Default Mode Network were not related to the mean change in noxious-evoked BOLD activity (Control Network: r = -0.36, p = 0.26, β = -0.25; Default Mode Network: r = 0.06, p = 0.88, β= -0.03 Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The mean functional connectivity in the Default Mode Network was not related to the mean change in noxious-evoked BOLD activity (r = 0.06, p = 0.88, β = -0.03).
source: In contrast, the mean functional connectivity in the Control Network and in the Default Mode Network were not related to the mean change in noxious-evoked BOLD activity (Control Network: r = -0.36, p = 0.26, β = -0.25; Default Mode Network: r = 0.06, p = 0.88, β= -0.03 Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The absence of a significant relationship between the functional connectivity of the Default Mode Network and the noxious-evoked BOLD activity suggests that the influence of the DPMS on the noxious-activity is not generalisable across all established brain networks.
source: The absence of a significant relationship between the functional connectivity of the Default Mode Network and the noxious-evoked BOLD activity suggests that the influence of the DPMS on the noxious-activity is not generalisable across all established brain networks.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the statistical results.

claim: Increased pre-stimulus functional connectivity between the ACC and PAG was associated with a substantial reduction in noxious-evoked BOLD activity (p = 0.0012, β = -0.22).
source: Increased pre-stimulus functional connectivity between the ACC and PAG was associated with a substantial reduction in noxious-evoked BOLD activity (adjusted for age, p = 0.0012, β = -0.22, Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Functional connectivity between the AI-mFG was strongly related to the change in noxious-evoked BOLD activity (p = 0.02, β = -0.23).
source: Functional connectivity between the AI-mFG and ACC-AI were also strongly related to the change in noxious-evoked BOLD activity (p = 0.02, β = -0.23 and p = 0.03, β = -0.17 respectively, Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: Functional connectivity between the ACC-AI was strongly related to the change in noxious-evoked BOLD activity (p = 0.03, β = -0.17).
source: Functional connectivity between the AI-mFG and ACC-AI were also strongly related to the change in noxious-evoked BOLD activity (p = 0.02, β = -0.23 and p = 0.03, β = -0.17 respectively, Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: For all other pairs of brain regions, the functional connectivity strength did not influence the magnitude of noxious-evoked brain activity.
source: For all other pairs of brain regions, the functional connectivity strength did not influence the magnitude of noxious-evoked brain activity.
evidence: This is a summary of the statistical analysis results.

claim: In adults, greater co-variation in the functional activity of the rostral ACC and PAG relates to an increase in the efficacy of endogenous analgesia elicited by placebo treatment.
source: The observation that a high degree of functional connectivity between the ACC and PAG is strongly associated with a reduction in pain-related brain activity in the infant is interesting in light of observations in adults where greater co-variation in the functional activity of the rostral ACC and PAG relates to an increase in the efficacy of endogenous analgesia elicited by placebo treatment (Petrovic et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Anticipation of placebo has been associated with greater pre-stimulus activity in the PAG, and leads to a placebo-induced reduction in evoked brain activity in the thalamus and rostral ACC.
source: Anticipation of placebo has been associated with greater pre-stimulus activity in the PAG, and leads to a placebo-induced reduction in evoked brain activity in the thalamus and rostral ACC (Wager et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Direct stimulation of the PAG is associated with a reduction in incoming nociceptive information from the peripheral nervous system in animal studies.
source: The importance of the PAG, as part of the DPMS, has also been demonstrated in animal studies, where direct stimulation of the PAG is associated with a reduction in incoming nociceptive information from the peripheral nervous system (Reynolds, 1969).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to animal studies.

claim: In adult rodents, descending modulation (evidenced by PAG activation) preferentially modulates C-fibre input.
source: In adult rodents, descending modulation (evidenced by PAG activation) preferentially modulates C-fibre input (McMullan and Lumb, 2006; Waters and Lumb, 2008), whereas the noxious stimulus applied in this study likely preferentially activates A-delta fibres, which may be differentially modulated compared with C fibre input.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to animal studies.

claim: The noxious stimulus applied in this study likely preferentially activates A-delta fibres.
source: In adult rodents, descending modulation (evidenced by PAG activation) preferentially modulates C-fibre input (McMullan and Lumb, 2006; Waters and Lumb, 2008), whereas the noxious stimulus applied in this study likely preferentially activates A-delta fibres, which may be differentially modulated compared with C fibre input.
evidence: This is an inference based on the characteristics of the stimulus used.

claim: A-delta fibres may be differentially modulated compared with C fibre input.
source: In adult rodents, descending modulation (evidenced by PAG activation) preferentially modulates C-fibre input (McMullan and Lumb, 2006; Waters and Lumb, 2008), whereas the noxious stimulus applied in this study likely preferentially activates A-delta fibres, which may be differentially modulated compared with C fibre input.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential differences in modulation.

claim: Human and non-human infants display heightened sensitivity to noxious stimulation.
source: Human and non-human infants display heightened sensitivity to noxious stimulation, which has long been attributed to hyper-excitable spinal reflex networks (Fitzgerald, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Heightened sensitivity to noxious stimulation in infants has long been attributed to hyper-excitable spinal reflex networks.
source: Human and non-human infants display heightened sensitivity to noxious stimulation, which has long been attributed to hyper-excitable spinal reflex networks (Fitzgerald, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: In the neonatal rodent, brain structures within the DPMS facilitate, rather than inhibit, spinally-mediated nocifensive behaviours.
source: In the neonatal rodent, brain structures within the DPMS facilitate, rather than inhibit, spinally-mediated nocifensive behaviours (Hathway et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to animal studies.

claim: During human preterm development, exaggerated reflexes are refined with shorter durations, lower magnitudes, and higher response thresholds.
source: During human preterm development, these exaggerated reflexes are refined with shorter durations, lower magnitudes, and higher response thresholds, and patterns of noxious-evoked brain activity concomitantly mature (Hartley et al., 2016; Cornelissen et al., 2013; Fabrizi et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Patterns of noxious-evoked brain activity concomitantly mature during human preterm development.
source: During human preterm development, these exaggerated reflexes are refined with shorter durations, lower magnitudes, and higher response thresholds, and patterns of noxious-evoked brain activity concomitantly mature (Hartley et al., 2016; Cornelissen et al., 2013; Fabrizi et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The data suggest that the functional DPMS brain networks have an inhibitory function at the level of the brain in term infants, similar to that observed in the adult.
source: The data presented here in term infants suggest that the functional DPMS brain networks have an inhibitory function at the level of the brain, similar to that observed in the adult (Ossipov et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: There is a potential contradiction with observations in neonatal rodents where facilitation at the level of the spinal cord has been observed in electrophysiological recordings.
source: There is, however, a potential contradiction with observations in neonatal rodents where facilitation at the level of the spinal cord has been observed in electrophysiological recordings.
evidence: This acknowledges a potential discrepancy between the current findings and prior animal research.

claim: The potential contradiction could reflect maturational differences in the connectivity of supraspinal DPMS regions and the connectivity of the descending pathways from the RVM to the spinal nociceptive dorsal horn network in newborn infants.
source: This could reflect maturational differences in the connectivity of supraspinal DPMS regions and the connectivity of the descending pathways from the RVM to the spinal nociceptive dorsal horn network in newborn infants.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the potential contradiction.

claim: This interpretation relies on a comparison across species, which is based on a theoretical age-equivalence between human infants and neonatal rat pups.
source: Nevertheless, this interpretation relies on a comparison across species, which is based on a theoretical age-equivalence between human infants and neonatal rat pups.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation in comparing across species.

claim: Some networks will likely have a different developmental trajectory in rodents compared with humans.
source: Some networks will likely have a different developmental trajectory in rodents compared with humans and the maturation of the CNS is not a coordinated linear process as different networks likely mature at different rates (Clancy et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The maturation of the CNS is not a coordinated linear process as different networks likely mature at different rates.
source: Some networks will likely have a different developmental trajectory in rodents compared with humans and the maturation of the CNS is not a coordinated linear process as different networks likely mature at different rates (Clancy et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The study did not measure activity in the spinal cord.
source: As we have not measured activity in the spinal cord, we cannot determine the relationship between functional connectivity in the DPMS and spinal activity in the term-aged infant.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the study.

claim: The study cannot determine the relationship between functional connectivity in the DPMS and spinal activity in the term-aged infant.
source: As we have not measured activity in the spinal cord, we cannot determine the relationship between functional connectivity in the DPMS and spinal activity in the term-aged infant.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the study.

claim: Collecting functional imaging data in the brainstem is challenging, both in adults and infants, due to head motion, and cardiac-related and respiratory-related motion.
source: Collecting functional imaging data in the brainstem is challenging, both in adults and infants, due to head motion, and cardiac-related and respiratory-related motion (Harita and Stroman, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Physiological noise was identified and regressed out using independent component analysis.
source: In this study, we identified and regressed out physiological noise using independent component analysis (Salimi-Khorshidi et al., 2014; McKeown et al., 2005; McKeown et al., 1998).
evidence: This describes a methodological approach used in the study.

claim: The strength of the DPMS Network within the cortical and subcortical regions (excluding brainstem) was significantly inversely related to noxious-evoked brain activity (r = -0.61, p = 0.04, β = -0.37).
source: The strength of the DPMS Network within the remaining cortical and subcortical regions, the ACC, AI, mFG and AMY, was still significantly inversely related to noxious-evoked brain activity (r = -0.61, p = 0.04, β = -0.37, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The Control Network excluding the PON was not significantly correlated with noxious-evoked brain activity (r = -0.29, p = 0.36, β = -0.15).
source: As before, the Control Network excluding the PON, was not significantly correlated with noxious-evoked brain activity (r = -0.29, p = 0.36, β = -0.15).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The results are unlikely to be driven by noise within the brainstem.
source: This suggests that our results are unlikely to be driven by noise within the brainstem.
evidence: This is an inference based on the analysis excluding brainstem regions.

claim: The PAG and RVM masks that were individually defined for each infant are well localised within these anatomical structures.
source: While there are inherent limitations in this study in terms of the spatial resolution that can be achieved when imaging small structures within the brainstem, we believe that the PAG and RVM masks that we individually defined for each infant are well localised within these anatomical structures.
evidence: This is a statement about the quality of the anatomical masks used.

claim: The stimulus presentation was not predictable.
source: It is possible that application of the noxious stimulus could influence the pre-stimulus data; however, the stimulus presentation was not predictable, and the time-period between stimuli was always greater than 25 s.
evidence: This describes a feature of the experimental design.

claim: The time-period between stimuli was always greater than 25 s.
source: It is possible that application of the noxious stimulus could influence the pre-stimulus data; however, the stimulus presentation was not predictable, and the time-period between stimuli was always greater than 25 s.
evidence: This describes a feature of the experimental design.

claim: The pre-stimulus functional connectivity of the DPMS was not dependent on stimulus number (p = 0.33, repeated measures ANOVA).
source: The pre-stimulus functional connectivity of the DPMS was not dependent on stimulus number (p = 0.33, repeated measures ANOVA, see Figure 1—figure supplement 3), suggesting that the functional connectivity of this network is relatively stable.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The functional connectivity of the DPMS network is relatively stable.
source: The pre-stimulus functional connectivity of the DPMS was not dependent on stimulus number (p = 0.33, repeated measures ANOVA, see Figure 1—figure supplement 3), suggesting that the functional connectivity of this network is relatively stable.
evidence: This is an inference based on the statistical analysis.

claim: In adults, functional brain networks are thought to be dominated by stable individual features, and only modestly influenced by evoked factors and day-to-day variability.
source: In adults, functional brain networks are also thought to be dominated by stable individual features, and only modestly influenced by evoked factors and day-to-day variability (Gratton et al., 2018).
